```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x)) y else x
```

## Why Wording Matters

SIEVER shows each item's **wording** (the actual question text) in the
Ingest grid (its Question column), the Items grid (its Wording column) and
the item detail pane, runs its deterministic item writing checks on it (the
Content Validity tab's Item Writing Checks), and can
gather a construct's wordings for review on the Items page (Prepare an
Expert Review Brief: read them as a written description, or copy the
structured brief into a large language model of your own choosing).
Seeing the wording while you work makes it far easier to group items into
the right constructs and to spot an item that does not belong.

When you load an SPSS `.sav` file, SIEVER reads the wording from each variable's
**variable label** automatically. This vignette shows the other ways to attach
wording when your data start life in R.

The single fact to remember: **SIEVER reads an item's wording from the column's
`"label"` attribute** (the same place `haven` puts an SPSS variable label). So
any route that sets `attr(column, "label")` will surface the wording in the app.

## 1. Build an Example Data Set and Attach Wordings in Base R

Here we simulate a tiny three-item data frame and attach each item's wording
with `attr()`.

```{r build}
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
dat <- data.frame(
  talk  = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE),
  party = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE),
  quiet = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE)
)

# Attach the actual item wording to each column's "label" attribute.
attr(dat$talk,  "label") <- "I start conversations."
attr(dat$party, "label") <- "I feel at ease around people at parties."
attr(dat$quiet, "label") <- "I keep in the background."   # reverse keyed

# Read them back:
vapply(dat, function(x) attr(x, "label") %||% NA_character_, character(1))
```

A column that has a `"label"` attribute behaves like a normal numeric column for
analysis, but SIEVER will display the label as the item's wording.

## 2. Attach Wordings With `labelled` / `haven`

If you prefer a tidyverse-style workflow, `labelled::var_label()` sets the
same attribute (so does `haven::labelled(x, label = "...")`, one column at
a time):

```{r labelled, eval = FALSE}
library(labelled)
var_label(dat) <- list(
  talk  = "I start conversations.",
  party = "I feel at ease around people at parties.",
  quiet = "I keep in the background."
)
```

## 3. Write a Labeled `.sav` So It Round-Trips Into the App

To load the wordings through SIEVER's normal `.sav` path, write the labeled data
with `haven`; the variable labels become the wordings when SIEVER reads the file.

```{r sav, eval = FALSE}
haven::write_sav(dat, "extraversion_items.sav")
# Then in the app: on Ingest, choose Data file alone in step 1, choose
# extraversion_items.sav, and press Load (step 2).
```

## 4. Supply Wording Through the Specification File

SIEVER records a study's *specification* in a small `.csv` with one row per
column of the data: its role, Item Name (`label`), **wording**, measurement
`type`, construct, facet, inclusion status, reverse keying and response
bounds. `sieve_specification_template()` writes the template with
everything SIEVER can propose filled in (here it reads the labels attached
above into both `label` and `wording`), and you edit the rest, in R or in a
spreadsheet. Its help page describes every column and the vocabulary each
one takes.

```{r spec}
spec <- SIEVER::sieve_specification_template(dat)
spec$type      <- "ordered"            # five point rating items
spec$construct <- "Extraversion"
spec$label     <- c("Talkative", "At ease at parties", "Stays in background")
spec$wording   <- c("I start conversations.",
                    "I feel at ease around people at parties.",
                    "I keep in the background.")
spec$reverse[spec$variable == "quiet"] <- "TRUE"
spec$rev_lo <- "1"                     # the response bounds a reversal reflects within
spec$rev_hi <- "5"
spec_file <- tempfile("extraversion_spec_", fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(spec, spec_file, row.names = FALSE)
spec[, c("variable", "label", "wording", "type", "construct", "reverse", "rev_lo", "rev_hi")]
```

The template proposes `continuous` for these items because each has five
distinct values (the detection rule the Ingest tab states: two distinct
values binary, three or four ordered, five or more continuous, following
Rhemtulla, Brosseau-Liard and Savalei, 2012); a five point rating scale is
ordered, so the type is corrected here. Note that the five-option rule is
on by default (the checkbox in step 1 of the Ingest tab, and
`continuous_from = 5` in `sieve_prepare_study()`) and reads an item typed
ordered with five or more response options as continuous, on the same
finding; to keep the categorical treatment, pass `continuous_from = NULL`
below (the types are then recorded as your own choice and kept when the
project is opened), and in the app turn the checkbox off before loading or
applying the file, or set Type to ordered in the grid afterward. Two routes
take the file into the app. In step 1 choose Data file with its
specification (two files, chosen together), choose the data file and the
specification in the file input, and press Load (step 2): the
specification sets the roles, Item Names, wordings, types, constructs,
facets, inclusion and keying, and because it types every item the study is
confirmed from it; or, with the data already loaded, open **Apply a
specification to the loaded data** in the Ingest sidebar and choose the
file under Specification file. The specification is matched by variable
name, and one with a problem (a variable not in the data, a type outside
the vocabulary) is refused as a whole and changes nothing. Without the app,
`sieve_prepare_study()` applies the same file through the same checks and
writes a project file, which opens on Ingest with Open project (shows what
the file holds first) or dropped into the data file input under
SIEVER-ready file, already confirmed:

```{r prepare}
study <- SIEVER::sieve_prepare_study(dat, spec,
                                     file = tempfile("extraversion_", fileext = ".siever.rds"),
                                     name = "Extraversion items",
                                     continuous_from = NULL)
```

Here the editable **Item Name** (`label`) is short, while the **Wording** is the
full text; renaming the Item Name in the app never loses the wording, because
the two are stored separately. After you have changed anything in the
grid, the Reproducible Code page's Download specification (.csv) writes
the current specification back out, so the file beside the data stays the
record of the study.

## 5. Confirm the Wording Reached the Ledger

Internally, SIEVER keeps a *ledger* with one row per item and a preserved
`wording` column. When you load data with labels attached, or apply a specification
with a `wording` column, that column is populated for you. The project
written above holds that ledger:

```{r ledger}
study$meta[, c("item", "label", "wording", "construct", "type", "reverse")]
```

The wording travels with each item through the whole pipeline: the
Content Validity tab's deterministic item writing checks read it
(`sieve_wording_checks()` is the same check from a script), the item
detail pane shows it, and the Items page's Prepare an Expert Review Brief
gathers it, per construct or for every construct, as a written description
or a structured brief.

## Summary

- SIEVER reads item wording from each column's `"label"` attribute.
- Set it in base R with `attr(col, "label") <- "..."`, or with
  `labelled::var_label()` / `haven::labelled()`.
- Write a labeled `.sav` to use the normal load path, or fill the
  `wording` column of the specification file that
  `sieve_specification_template()` writes and apply it on Ingest (or
  through `sieve_prepare_study()`).
- The wording is shown throughout the app, checked on the Content Validity
  tab, and gathered on the Items page, per construct or
  for the whole instrument, for a written description or an expert review
  brief.
